Retrieval remains a major bottleneck when useful information is preserved, suggesting that improving access to existing information may be at least as important as constructing richer explicit memory.
items.author: Yongjie Zhou, Shuai Wang, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon

items.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24614v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.
items.author: Chengyu Xie, Fei Shen, Shuyi Miao, Yue Feng, Jian Yu, Pengyang Shao, Yijun Tian, Xiaoyu Du

items.title: EGIP: An Evidence-Grounded Interaction Protocol for Clinical Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interactive clinical agents acquire evidence through patient dialogue and diagnostic examinations, yet their performance also depends on how the interaction environment exposes information, available actions, and examination results. When these conditions are implicit or inconsistently controlled, final-answer accuracy can conflate diagnostic reasoning with the effects of the interaction protocol. We propose the \textbf{E}vidence-\textbf{G}rounded \textbf{I}nteraction \textbf{P}rotocol (EGIP), which enforces role-specific information boundaries, exposes diagnostic actions without revealing their results, retrieves examination results from stored clinical records, and organizes acquired evidence for final decision-making. By separating evidence acquisition from terminal prediction, EGIP enables different decision strategies to operate on the same observations. We evaluate EGIP across two clinical-agent frameworks, five datasets, and six language models. EGIP improves diagnostic accuracy over native baselines across all primary comparisons. A clinician review further shows that the proportion of automatically scored correct responses jointly judged evidence-supported rises from 10.20\% to 36.55\%. These findings support the effectiveness of EGIP as a unified interaction protocol for improving clinical-agent performance through controlled evidence access and acquisition.
items.author: Zecheng Ren, Ruichen Cong, Yi Min Chen, Jing Zhang, Feiyang Chen, Wutong Zhang, Kaixiang Wang, Zihan Wang, Jiong Lou, Jie LI, Qun Jin

items.title: Backend-Frontend Converter: Component-Based Conversion of .NET Computational Models to TypeScript
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24492v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational models developed in .NET often need to run locally within web applications. We present Backend--Frontend Converter, an architecture for generating TypeScript implementations of component-based models. The converter maps components, connections, aliases, and formula trees to model-specific TypeScript code. Reusable runtime libraries provide numerical integration, data access, and state handling. We evaluate stored generated implementations through four orbital scenarios and a recorded trading-strategy comparison. Orbital calculations execute in a browser and are paired with C\# results by crossing event and timestamp; trading outputs are aligned by date. Analytic scheduler tests and deliberately perturbed outputs assess the validation procedure. Each orbital scenario produces 91 paired events with identical timestamps. Position and velocity differences remain below $(10^{-6}\)~km$ and $(10^{-9}\)~km/s$. All 20 analytic scheduler checks pass, and the comparator detects each of three prescribed state and time perturbations. The trading comparison contains 501 aligned daily records with matching indicator values, positions, and order events. The evaluated implementations preserve the compared outputs across the C#/TypeScript boundary. Component-specific generation and reusable execution libraries provide a practical route from supported .NET computational models to TypeScript applications.
items.author: Petr Ivankov (Independent researcher), Max Shestov (Georgia Institute of Technology)

items.title: Vocal-Tract Acoustics, Aerodynamics, and Overlap-and-Add Synthesis in DYNARTmo
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24490v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents the acoustic and aerodynamic extension of DYNARTmo, a dynamic articulatory model for visualizing and synthesizing speech production. Gestural control trajectories determine vocal-tract geometry, which is converted into an acoustic tube with nasal branching and effective lateral passages. A lumped aerodynamic network relates prescribed glottal motion and pulmonary pressure to airflow and supraglottal pressure storage. Phonatory excitation, oral friction, and glottal aspiration are synthesized as separate contributions. Frame-specific acoustic responses are combined by overlap-and-add, preserving response tails beyond individual control frames. Three German words, ``Tasse'', ``Muse'', and ``Lade'', illustrate the coordination of articulation, pressure, flow, and acoustic sources across vowels, nasals, laterals, fricatives, and plosives. The implementation has been optimized by the author primarily for sound recognizability; independent perceptual evaluation remains outstanding, and fricative-noise naturalness requires further refinement. The model provides an inspectable, articulatorily controlled production plant for future neural simulations of babbling, imitation, and early word acquisition. Further work will improve acoustic realism, reduce empirical source corrections, and extend the sensory information available to developmental learning models.
items.author: Bernd J. Kr\"oger

items.title: Modeling Discourse Profiles in Climate Misinformation Discourse
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24489v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Prior work on climate misinformation detection typically classifies individual comments or claims using text alone. This framing overlooks a key property of online climate discourse: misinformation is often produced, reinforced, and sustained through recurring rhetorical patterns that reappear across comments and threads. Using a large-scale TikTok climate discourse dataset, we construct discourse profiles by clustering climate-related comments into recurring rhetorical patterns. We then incorporate these profiles into fine-grained climate misinformation classifiers using a late-fusion architecture. Under video-disjoint evaluation across three training seeds, discourse-profile-aware models significantly improve macro-F1 over text-only baselines for bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and MPNet representations. RoBERTa-large exhibits a positive mean improvement but substantially greater variability, and the difference is not statistically significant. Beyond classification, our results show discourse profiles shape misinformation reception and propagation. Discourse-profile-conditioned language model agents exhibit misinformation acceptance patterns aligned with profile-level misinformation prevalence in ClimateDisc, and the relationship between misinformation prevalence and engagement persistence differs across dominant discourse profiles.
items.author: Ge Gao, Zhengyang Shan, Bryan A. Plummer, Margrit Betke, Derry Wijaya

items.title: Beyond Recall Saturation: Scaling Hard-Negative Reranker Training for Industrial Legal Retrieval
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24478v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial retrieval systems often improve quality by enlarging embedding candidate pools or adopting complex training pipelines. We show that, under a sufficiently large but practical candidate pool, embedding recall exhibits diminishing returns, motivating a closer examination of reranker quality. On Chinese legal retrieval benchmarks, embedding top-300 reaches a high-recall operating region, while relevant evidence may still be ranked below the output cutoff. We compare hard-negative strategies for reranker training, including embedding-mined, self-mined, and dynamic-negative variants, under aligned retrieval protocols that evaluate reranking after candidate retrieval. Among the evaluated staged configurations, an embedding-to-self-mined pipeline provides a favorable trade-off; additional dynamic stages do not improve all held-out metrics. The selected pipeline scales from a 0.6B to a 4B reranker. Relative to the native 4B reranker, the trained 4B Stage2 model improves reported metrics on the STARD and CSAID benchmarks and on an internal development set, and is preferred in 72.4\% of non-tied comparisons on 410 de-identified, reconstructed internal operational-query inputs in a latency-sensitive offline preference evaluation. These results support evaluating the retrieval and reranking stages separately when selecting an optimization target for industrial retrieval systems.
items.author: Yunhan Li, Mingjie Xie, Zeyang Shi, Gengshen Wu, Min Yang

items.title: Ben-Misandry: A Bengali Dataset and Late-Fusion Transformer Framework for Detecting Anti-Male Gender Hate
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24474v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gender based hate speech research in Bengali has focused almost exclusively on misogyny, leaving anti male hate, or misandry, entirely unstudied for this language and creating a systematic blind spot in moderation systems trained to catch attacks on women but not on men. We introduce Ben-Misandry, the first Bengali misandry detection dataset: 5,000 comments across six taxonomy classes, including a novel category for mocking male emotional vulnerability with no direct analogue in existing misogyny taxonomies. The corpus is taxonomy-controlled synthetic data generated with GPT-4.1, spot-checked by four human reviewers on a 500-comment sample who confirmed the large majority of assigned labels; a full inter-annotator- agreement study is left to future work. We benchmark it with a classical pipeline (seven classifiers over four text representations) and a transformer pipeline (BanglaBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, and two fusion strategies). The best classical model, a linear SVM over character-level TF-IDF, reaches 91.8% accuracy; a late fusion ensemble averaging BanglaBERT and XLM-RoBERTa softmax outputs reaches 96.6% accuracy and macro ROC-AUC above 99%, nominally ahead of every single model and early fusion, though we have not run significance testing to confirm these margins are meaningful. We relate this to classifier combination theory, under which averaging encoders with decorrelated errors is expected to reduce variance, and corroborate the decision boundary with Shapley explanations that recover the same class- discriminative vocabulary found in our exploratory analysis, while noting this cannot rule out the model partly keying on synthetic-generation artifacts. Our results indicate misandry detection in Bengali is feasible and measurable on this synthetic corpus, offered as an initial public resource pending validation on real-world data.
items.author: Md Mehedi Hasan Nipu, Chinmoy Mitra, Tarannum Ahmed Nowshin, Israt Moyeen Noumi

items.title: Toward a Universal Local Speech Feature Extractor Through Distillation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised speech models commonly consist of a set of convolutional neural network (CNN) layers used as a local feature extractor, followed by transformer layers. The CNN layers are computationally demanding, and are also similar across models and resemble the much simpler mel spectral features. We hypothesize that the CNN layers can be replaced by a simple, universal model. To test this hypothesis, we learn a two-layer feature extractor via distillation from one or more teacher models (HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM). Experiments on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks show that our model largely retains the performance of the teacher models and can also be used in an unseen model (wav2vec 2.0). Our feature extractor requires only 3% of the MACs of the CNNs, resulting in a $>$20% overall inference runtime reduction.
items.author: Jessica Yang, Marcelo Beramendi Caballero, Ju-Chieh Chou, Karen Livescu

items.title: Ask Less, Ask Better: Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents can ask clarifying questions to complete tasks, but answering each question demands users' time and effort. Existing evaluations typically measure this burden by counting questions, treating necessary and avoidable questions equally. We propose an evaluation protocol that distinguishes how often agents ask from how well they ask. An interruption budget limits the number of questions, while a user-attention cost charges extra for questions that are hard to read or not worth asking, as rated by a human-validated LLM judge. Beyond question counts, this cost captures perceived effort: on conversation pairs with the same number of questions, human annotators agreed with the cost on which conversation required more effort 75% of the time. Across eight LLMs and four customer-service domains, limiting agents to one to three questions reduces user-attention cost by 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the task reward they earn with unlimited questions. At the same budget, reviewing each question against the memory of users' earlier answers cuts attention cost by another 13% with little reward loss and yields more valuable questions. Models also differ sharply in how well they ask: at the same user-attention cost, the most efficient models gain more than twice as much reward from their questions as the others. These results show that asking less and asking better are distinct goals, and that evaluations of proactive agents should measure both.
items.author: Xuanming Zhang, Amir H. Rezaeian, Miguel Ballesteros, Weiyi Sun, Werner Geyer, Lydia B. Chilton, Zhou Yu, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth

items.title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24365v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter-token dependencies. On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.
items.author: Jeff Shen, Zhejian Zhou, Ryan Lee, Jonathan May, Shirley Ho

items.title: Beyond Clean Accuracy: The Practical Challenges and Benefits of Pixel-Based Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24290v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pixel-based language models process rendered text without relying on a fixed subword vocabulary, offering a promising approach to noisy and multilingual inputs. However, their practical value depends on whether they can be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. To this end, we systematically examine this question through fine-tuning behavior, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Under our tested settings, pixel-based models require longer training and broader labelled-data coverage than text-based models, while delayed learning and learning-rate-dependent failures make adaptation less reliable. Our analyses further suggest that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations, placing greater demands on fine-tuning. Once successfully adapted, however, pixel-based models lose substantially less accuracy under typographical noise and achieve higher target-language accuracy than English-pretrained text-based counterparts on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean English performance. Together, these findings reveal a central trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but shifts a central bottleneck to downstream adaptation.
items.author: Haowen Tang, Wei Xia, Raoyuan Zhao, Hinrich Sch\"utze, Yihong Liu

items.title: Modeling bilingual naming performance through laterally-connected SOMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24275v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational models have explanatory power to understand cognition in individuals, but there is usually not enough training data to build such models with traditional machine learning. However, alternative architectures that model neural and cognitive processes in more detail can be more easily fit to individuals and can lead to mechanistic insights into human behavior. BiLex is such a computational model of the bilingual lexicon, containing a shared semantic system and phonetic language systems represented through self-organizing maps. In this study, BiLex was extended further into biological realism with excitatory and inhibitory lateral connections. This extension makes it possible to account for response times as well as common errors such as those based on semantic concept familiarity, typicality, and specificity. The Boston Naming Test was simulated in Spanish and English, and model performance approximated naming accuracy and error types in Spanish-English bilinguals with varying primary and secondary language histories. The results indicated that the approach captures semantic-level processes in bilingual lexical access, thus modeling the semantic cognition of individual subjects. In the future, such models may serve as a foundation for modeling impairments and treatment options.
items.author: Divya Prabhakaran, Uli Grasemann, Erie Shivers, Marissa Russell-Meill, Swathi Kiran, Risto Miikkulainen

items.title: Best of Both Worlds: Fine-Tuned Small Models Complement LLMs for Cost and Performance Benefits
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24260v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: BERT-based models require thousands of labeled samples to train. Larger models like GPT-X require only 1-5 examples per class. However, performance, cost and time tradeoffs of such models remain under-explored. In this work, we classify survey text data into 16 classes. We focus on experimental approaches and results on performance, cost, and time taken for this problem. We compare these parameters of a trained RoBERTa-based model, and an (off-the-shelf) GPT-3.5 model for text classification. Baseline experiments show that the time taken by GPT-3.5 for generating predictions on 10,000 records is 6 hours, whereas a RoBERTa-based model takes only 12 mins on a T4 GPU. To identify the best prompting approach for GPT-3.5, we explore batch prompting. We experiment with (1) batch-size, and (2) few-shot sampling. We find the best batch size is 20 with human few-shot curation. Experiments show the F1 score of a trained RoBERTa-based model (96%) is much higher than a GPT-3.5 model (83%). In case of GPT-3.5, batch prompting is beneficial in lowering inference costs by ~70%, without hindering task performance. We find the best approach is an ensemble of a RoBERTa-based and GPT-3.5 model (F1: 97.5%) incurring only 4.4% of inference cost compared to a standalone GPT-3.5.
items.author: Shivam Mathur, Sri Harish Popuri, Priya Krishnan Sundararajan, Kevin Horecka, Michael Mugo

items.title: SLA-LENS: From Classroom Transcripts to CSLA-Informed and Evidence-Linked L2 Interaction Analytics
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24259v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: What happens after a learner makes an error, and how does the instructor's response shape the next turn? Investigating these exchanges across classrooms requires context-sensitive annotation that is difficult to scale manually. We introduce SLA-LENS, an end-to-end LLM-assisted framework that connects classroom transcripts to structured pedagogical annotations and evidence-linked descriptive analytics. Grounded in interactionist Second Language Acquisition (SLA) theory, its annotation schema captures second language learner errors, pedagogical functions, and uptake or repair while accounting for speaker roles, conversational context, and hierarchical labels. We apply the framework to 40 authentic online L2 Spanish classroom transcripts comprising over 21,000 sentence-level instances. We evaluate proprietary and open-weight LLMs, including task-specific QLoRA adaptation, using expert-reviewed gold annotations, held-out silver data, and metrics sensitive to different types of annotation error. A deterministic reporting layer generates reproducible visualizations of participation, feedback, learner errors, uptake, and temporal interaction patterns, linked to supporting transcript evidence. By making these patterns accessible and inspectable, SLA-LENS supports systematic classroom discourse research, pedagogical reflection, and curriculum design.
items.author: Nemika Tyagi, Olga Kellert, Phanos Kareen, Nelvin Licona-Guevara

items.title: Language Models are Lazy Poets: Creative Mode Collapse at Scale
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24223v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While aligned large language models (LLMs) can successfully complete many creative tasks, their outputs tend to be highly self-similar. Though solutions to this problem of "mode collapse" have been proposed, comprehensive large-scale surveys of the phenomenon in specific textual genres are still lacking. We address this gap through an extensive treatment of LLM mode collapse in poetry. Across 15 poetic forms, 248 subject matter tags, and 16 open-weight models, we generate over 1.1 million poems. To our knowledge, this constitutes the largest corpus of LLM-generated poetry to date. At million-poem scale, we find that LLM poetic vocabularies and rhyming abilities are substantial, but severely underutilized. In other words, LLMs are "lazy" poets: despite possessing large poetic inventories, LLMs over-rely on a small number of words, opening phrases, and rhymes. Further, we find that lexical homogenization differs across models and poetic forms, noting observed rhyming vocabulary is correlated with model size.
items.author: Jacob A. Matthews, Sil Hamilton

items.title: Reasoning with Context Management and External Memory
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24187v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning models maintain information about the status of their reasoning process through in-context memory. Complex problems require larger context windows and memory requirements. In this scenario, context management without caching risks discarding useful information for reasoning. We propose RCMEM, an approach that extends context management with an external memory to maintain additional information without burdening the reasoning model with additional context. RCMEM significantly reduces computation time on problems that require repeated computation of intermediate steps, while achieving better performance on complex problems. We demonstrate our approach on a few mathematics problems using model sizes ranging from 0.4 to 25 million parameters, and GPT-2.
items.author: Man-Ling Sung, William Hartmann, Jiangying Zhou

items.title: Multi-author style detection with stylistic embeddings
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24184v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multi-author style change detection. Using off-the-shelf LLMs or supervised fine-tuning solely within the target domain fails to yield effective features; for this reason, we propose cross-domain transfer learning with LLM-based embeddings fine-tuned for authorship verification. We fine-tune Mistral-7B embedding model and compare it with DeBERTa, used in the state-of-the-art (SOTA) systems in PAN-25 multi-author writing style analysis challenge. Results show that DeBERTa and Mistral excel in different user-generated text scenarios. We exploit this diversity by combining both embeddings, leading to more effective style change detection.
items.author: Man-Ling Sung, Chak Fai Li, Damianos Karakos, Fred Bernardin, Brian Ulicny

items.title: Prosodic Structure as a Critical Component in Phonemic Language Modelling at BabyLM Scale
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human children learn language from continuous, prosodically structured speech long before they can read, yet almost all language models train on orthographic text. Building on previous phonemic BabyLM training (Goriely et al., 2024; arXiv:2410.22906), we ask whether supplying an estimate of the prosody infants exploit improves phonemic language modelling at BabyLM scale. We compare an orthographic baseline to three conditions forming a ladder of phonological richness. All conditions are trained as BERT MLMs at 10M and 100M words. Addressing the ecological validity of existing metrics in the small-data regime, we build a lexical decision task and two semantic organisation tasks. Our new lexical decision task offers improved insights into the distinction between wordlikeness, token familiarity, and lexicality as factors. Triphone phonotactic control and pseudo-log-likelihood scoring shows that these scores reflect phonotactic familiarity rather than wordhood: every model sits near or below chance on an adversarial inverted condition, revealing prior results of this kind as partly artefactual. On our new semantic tasks, a prosodically annotated phoneme stream gives the strongest taxonomic organisation at both the 10M and 100M word scales. Phonemic models with boundary structure are competitive with the orthographic baseline. These findings suggest that prosodic structure is a key component of phonemic language modelling in the small-data regime most analogous to infant learning.
items.author: Bill K. S. Ku, Janet B. Pierrehumbert

items.title: Pronouncing Hard Words: Phoneme Adaptation of a Pretrained Conversational Text to Speech Model
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Voice agents built as cascaded automatic speech recognition (ASR)->large language model (LLM)-> text-to-speech (TTS) pipelines increasingly rely on conversational TTS: streaming, context conditioned models that adapt delivery to dialogue history. Such models are natural and expressive but offer little explicit control over how rare, trust-critical drug names are pronounced, because these entities are too infrequent, and their vocabulary too fast-growing, to be covered by any amount of pre-, mid-, or post-training. We retrofit phoneme controllability onto a pretrained conversational TTS model without any pre/mid-training, using an ARPAbet vocabulary exten-sion, continued phoneme-augmented supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a training-free inference-time acoustic-biasing step. On a 7,500 clip clinical drug-pronunciation evaluation, our model raises strict Gemini-judged correctness from 54.6% (no phoneme augmentation) to 90.7%, outperforming every conversational and stateless TTS baseline on the automatic metric. Because no training stage sees a drug name, the entire evaluation is out-of-domain, so the gains reflect learned pronunciation rather than memorization. In a blinded, randomized human study, adult listeners judge 84% of our clips correct, versus 82% for the strongest baseline, with overlapping confidence intervals on a stratified subset. Across all 250 matched clips, Gemini agrees with the human majority on 84.8% of binary labels (k{appa}=0.57).
items.author: Yashish M. Siriwardena, Dinesh K. Gnanasekaran, Tanmay Laud, Shinji Watanabe, Subhabrata Mukherjee, Shanil Puri

items.title: Preservation and loss of algorithmic structure in experimental diffusion of joint-action norms
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24150v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Everyday norms of social interaction - e.g. norms of sharing space, taking turns, or queuing - are essential to large societies, offering structured procedures for common interactions. However, it remains unclear how the underlying algorithms of these implicit joint plans evolve as they diffuse through populations. Here we show that this process of diffusion can select against complex algorithms in the earliest stages. We conducted a large-scale study of experimental diffusion of novel social norms among human participants, leveraging advances in program synthesis to characterize the procedures people developed in independent populations. Inherited procedures became structurally simplified and lost during interactions between participants who inherited different variants of joint-action norms; however, opportunities for interactive repair offset this pressure, preserving complex algorithms despite misalignment. These results demonstrate that interactive reasoning mediates selective pressures on structural complexity during cultural evolution of procedural norms.
items.author: Dhara Yu, Bill D. Thompson

items.title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.24050v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
items.author: Junkai Zhou, Jiajia Wu, Zhaoyi Zhang, Shiting Guan, Chuanguang Yang

items.title: Translating in style: An open-weight alternative to GPT-4 for culturally aligned machine translation
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.23868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine translation systems often preserve meaning but systematically flatten linguistic style, a failure that is most acute when translating into non-Western languages. The RASTA framework of Havaldar et al. (2025a) addresses this through retrieval-augmented stylistic alignment, but relies on GPT-4, a closed, proprietary model. We investigate whether an open-weight translation specialist, Hunyuan-MT-7B, can serve as an open-weight alternative. We evaluate three variants of the model, the base model, a LoRA supervised fine-tune, and a GRPO-steered policy. We do this across three style dimensions (formality, politeness, and intimacy) and twelve directed language pairs, measuring style alignment with the correlation-based metric $\mathcal{A}$. We find that fine-tuning does not reliably improve alignment: the three variants are statistically indistinguishable in aggregate. The open backbone does not match RASTA-GPT-4 overall, but the shortfall is concentrated in formality and largely closes for intimacy and Chinese directions, where the open model matches or surpasses GPT-4 on individual pairs. An accessible RASTA pipeline built on an open model is thus already viable for parts of the problem.
items.author: Thomas Rietman, Hadi Mohammadi, Robert A. Bagheri

items.title: Modeling Human Behavior in the Prisoner's Dilemma with Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2610.23860v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Prisoner's Dilemma has long served as a foundational framework for studying human decision-making and cooperative outcomes across social scenarios, yet human behavior consistently deviates from predictions of fully rational economic theory. Previous works have studied human and LLM outcomes in the Prisoner's Dilemma; however, these studies have lacked at least one key feature: a memory component for LLM agents, accessible open-source models, or comparison against empirical human data. This project investigates whether open-source LLMs, TII Falcon 7B Instruct, Google Gemma 7B, Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Microsoft Phi Mini MoE Instruct, and Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, can model human cooperation patterns in repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, while examining how an LLM's knowledge that its opponent will be shuffled affects its decisions. Using a standardized prompting framework, we simulated interactions in two trial types: a fixed-partner setting where both agents retain memory, and a shuffled-partner setting where a memory-enabled agent, informed that its opponent changes across rounds, interacts with a memoryless agent. For each trial, we measured cooperation rates over 100 rounds and 10-round increments and compared them to human data from Montero-Porras et al. (2022). Under both frameworks, all LLMs differed from the human cooperation rate. Open-source LLMs generally over-cooperated relative to humans, particularly in the shuffled framework, where human cooperation averaged 28.5% while several models exceeded 80%. Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct showed deterministic tendencies, while Phi-mini-MoE-Instruct displayed greater variability and briefly approximated human rates. These findings suggest that LLMs have potential as behavioral simulation agents and provide a benchmark across two interaction environments, although open-source models are not yet reliable substitutes for human participants.
items.author: Raina Gao, Tristan Raffo

items.title: Mutual Information Constrained Chernoff Bottleneck
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.37994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The classical information bottleneck (IB) measures the relevance of a representation $U$ of $X$ to a target $Y$ by $I(U;Y)$, which does not directly characterize the error of downstream decisions. For a binary hypothesis $Y$ inferred from many separately encoded observations, the optimal error exponent is the Chernoff information between the two conditional distributions of $U$ given $Y$. We study the mutual information constrained Chernoff bottleneck, which seeks an encoder that maximizes this Chernoff information subject to a rate constraint $I(U;X) \leq R$. We show that its optimal value $C(R)$ increases strictly up to $R = H(V)$, where $V$ merges the symbols of $X$ with equal likelihood ratio, remains at the uncompressed exponent beyond, and, unlike the IB curve, need not be concave. We further show that $k+1$ outputs suffice to attain $C(R)$, where $k$ is the cardinality of $V$. We propose an alternating algorithm that updates the encoder via a generalized Blahut--Arimoto algorithm and the Chernoff parameter $s$ via a nonlinear equation, and prove that its iterates remain feasible, with nondecreasing and convergent Chernoff information. Comparing with the classical IB for $n$ samples, we show that, whenever the two objectives disagree, the IB encoder has the smaller equivocation $H(Y|U^{n})$ at $n = 1$, whereas the Chernoff bottleneck has the smaller error probability and equivocation for all large $n$. Numerical experiments confirm the theory, and on real topic-detection data from the 20 Newsgroups corpus, compressing each word to only $17\%$ of its entropy retains $90\%$ of the error exponent and nearly the accuracy of the uncompressed classifier.
items.author: Dier Tang, Guangyue Han

items.title: A Splitting Method for SDE Terminal-Law Estimation
items.summary:
arXiv:2609.12513v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In many settings involving stochastic differential equations (SDEs), including diffusion based generative AI, our aim is to accurately generate samples from a distribution. Typically, this is done by generating i.i.d. samples of the SDE. Given a fixed simulation budget, a reasonable way to gain efficiency may be to instead generate a tree of paths through appropriately split partial paths. This suggests improved performance, but one worries about the injected dependence. In this paper, we study this issue comprehensively. We develop a general method to construct the splitting design and analyze its performance for a broad class of error measures, giving insight into the elegant underlying structure in the problem. For the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), we identify the limiting errors of the associated empirical distributions as the simulation budget increases to infinity. We characterize a splitting strategy motivated by a corresponding asymptotic optimization problem. Overall, we observe a 12-26% improvement in mean KS over i.i.d. samples in many settings. On CIFAR-10 and FFHQ, splitting lowers the MMD by 17-26% relative to i.i.d. samples.
items.author: Rushil Gupta, Sandeep Juneja

items.title: Propensity Straight-Through Gradients for Discrete Stochastic Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.25631v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce the propensity straight-through (PST) estimator for gradient-based learning through exact simulations of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs). These models describe discrete stochastic dynamics across physics, chemistry, and biology, but their categorical event choices prevent ordinary differentiation. PST preserves exact forward trajectories and differentiates, in the backward pass, the normalized reaction propensities the simulator already computes. The affine state update makes this rule exact for the one-step conditional-mean sensitivity. We derive the per-step discrepancy for one-step sensitivities composed along nonlinear trajectories in closed form, show that it vanishes for affine downstream dependence, and bound it quadratically in the stoichiometric jump size. Across reversible dimerization, a genetic oscillator, a 50-task repressilator suite, and experimental patch-clamp recordings, PST recovers parameters to within 0.06-1.7% and converges 2.4-3.0-fold faster than the Gumbel-Softmax straight-through estimator at matched computational cost. At deep-learning scale, PST trains all 203,796 parameters of a stochastic reaction network using exact discrete events from initialization. By differentiating an exact conditional mean, PST eliminates reaction-selection temperature tuning and provides a scalable route to learning through exact stochastic dynamics.
items.author: Jose M. G. Vilar, Leonor Saiz

items.title: Parameterized Complexity of $L_p$-Lipschitz Constants for Input Convex Neural Networks and $L_p$-Norm Maximization over Zonotopes
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.24865v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Lipschitz constants are a standard way to quantify the sensitivity of neural networks to small input perturbations, but computing them is difficult even for shallow ReLU networks. We study this problem for two-layer input-convex neural networks (ICNNs), a restricted architecture where nonnegative output weights enforce convexity. Computing the $L_p$-Lipschitz constant for these networks is equivalent to maximizing the dual norm over a zonotope. While $L_1$- and $L_\infty$-norm maximization on zonotopes admit fixed-parameter and polynomial-time algorithms, respectively, the parameterized complexity of the remaining $L_p$-norms was open. We prove that, for every fixed $p\in (1,\infty)\cap \mathbb{Q}$, maximizing the $L_p$-norm over a zonotope in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is W[1]-hard with respect to the dimension $d$. Moreover, our hardness results imply that brute-force enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal for this problem under the Exponential Time Hypothesis. By duality, the same hardness results hold for computing the $L_p$-Lipschitz constant of two-layer ReLU ICNNs. Our proof first establishes the result for the $L_2$-norm and then transfers the construction to arbitrary fixed $p\in (1,\infty)\cap\mathbb{Q}$ using a suitable Taylor approximation. These results resolve the corresponding questions regarding the parameterized complexity status for zonotope norm maximization and two-layer ICNN Lipschitz constants.
  Our paper resolves an open problem posted at COLT'25. There are several independent concurrent papers resolving the same problem. Our paper prioritizes a clear exposition of the underlying mathematics and conceptual intuitions behind the proof. Additionally, we explicitly describe our research process including the use of LLMs.
items.author: Aritra Das, Vincent Froese, Moritz Grillo, Debayan Gupta, Christoph Hertrich, Tharrshann Jayan Logarajah, Georg Loho, Mihir More, Moritz Stargalla

items.title: Arbitrage-Aware Probabilistic Multi-Step Forecasting of Implied Volatility Surfaces: Joint Generation of Surface-Return Trajectories Using Latent Diffusion
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.22478v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Implied volatility surfaces summarise the option market and are central to many financial applications. Probabilistic forecasting of their future evolution requires modelling two-dimensional geometry, temporal dependence, and predictive uncertainty while preserving economic admissibility. We propose a conditional latent diffusion framework for generating joint 30-step trajectories of implied volatility surfaces and underlying returns. An arbitrage-aware autoencoder learns a surface representation, while diffusion captures the evolution. Evaluated on SPX surfaces, the framework generates realistic probabilistic multi-step scenarios. Its predictive mean also outperforms persistence beyond the shortest horizons.
items.author: Dominik Manuel Buchegger, Lukas Gonon

items.title: Advanced Linear Algebra with Applications - Part I (Numerical linear algebra for PDEs, machine learning, and data assimilation)
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.21234v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: These lecture notes form the first part of a master's-level course on advanced numerical linear algebra. Their aim is not only to present the classical algorithms, but to show why the subject has become considerably more central than it was a generation ago. Numerical linear algebra grew up alongside the numerical solution of partial differential equations, and for a long time that is where its large sparse systems came from. Ranking the nodes of a network, assimilating observations into a weather forecast, and fitting a model to a large noisy data set now lead to problems of the same kind: too large to factorise, structured, and accessible only through matrix-vector products. Strikingly few ideas are needed for all of them. Each chapter therefore develops a standard topic and then puts it to work outside its original setting. We treat norms, factorisations, conditioning and floating-point arithmetic; sparse matrices arising from finite differences, from graphs and from machine learning; stationary iterations and the smoothing property; the conjugate gradient and Lanczos methods, with spectral clustering and regularisation by early stopping; Arnoldi and GMRES, with PageRank and large least squares; and finally preconditioning, Schwarz domain decomposition and multigrid. We assume a first course in linear algebra. Every section closes with a summary of what should be retained and every chapter with exercises, several drawn from past examinations. Accompanying Python code reproduces the numerical illustrations.
items.author: Victorita Dolean, Jemima Tabeart

items.title: Harmonic Torsional Diffusion for Protein-Ligand Flexible Docking
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.20366v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Molecular docking requires reasoning jointly about ligand pose and protein flexibility. Most diffusion-based docking models predict torsional updates with generic Euclidean heads that ignore the periodic geometry of angular variables. This mismatch is especially limiting in flexible docking, where ligand conformations and pocket side chains co-adapt to form the bound complex. Here, we introduce Harmony, a harmonic torsional diffusion framework for flexible protein-ligand docking. Harmony parameterizes ligand and side-chain torsional score fields as derivatives of learned harmonic potentials on the circle, which are noised mode by mode in the Fourier basis owing to the properties of variance-exploding diffusion on the torus. This construction makes periodicity explicit and gives the model a frequency-aware inductive bias over rotameric motion. On the PDBBind benchmark, Harmony improves ligand pose accuracy and pocket all-atom reconstruction over recent flexible docking methods. On PoseBusters, it improves the physical validity of generated complexes. Case studies on EBNA1 and KRAS G12D illustrate the method's behavior on a polar and a shallow binding site, respectively. Together, these results indicate that aligning the score parameterization with the geometry of the diffusion process is a simple and effective lever for improving flexible docking.
items.author: Maksim Zhdanov, Pavel Strashnov, Vladislav Kurenkov

items.title: Gravitational-wave parameter estimation with machine-learning generated surrogate waveforms
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.20222v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The worldwide network of gravitational-wave detectors have detected more than 350 binary coalescence events till date. Future third-generation detectors, like Einstein telescope, are expected to detect orders-of-magnitude more signals from sources with more complicated characteristics, including eccentric orbits and high-mass ratio binaries. It is well-established that the computational cost of parameter estimation for signals from these kinds of sources will be extremely high. In particular, the process could be sped-up if generating theoretical waveform predictions, used for likelihood calculation becomes faster. Recently, various machine-learning techniques has been proposed to this end. In this work, we propose a two-stage deterministic conditional-autoencoder model for generating four-parameter SEOBNRv4 waveforms. The first-stage of the model generates amplitude and phase series of the waveform, while the second-stage calibrates the residual error in the predictions. Our model achieves a median mismatch of around $10^{-2}$ with the target polarization waveforms, while the calibrated amplitude/phase series achieve $10^{-6}$ level cosine distance error. We then propose a waveform conditioning step to enable use of these surrogate waveforms for downstream parameter estimation tasks. Finally, we perform extensive parameter estimation tests, with ML and EOB waveform injections and try to recover posterior estimates for the source parameters. We find that when ML waveforms are used to recover EOB target parameter estimates, the inferred posterior have some systematic bias. This inherent bias can be estimated and corrected for, and then importance reweighting of posterior samples can enable use of low-accuracy surrogate waveforms at low SNRs.
items.author: Suyog Garg, Kipp Cannon

items.title: What Does It Take For A Generalist Robot Policy To Adapt From Minimal Data?
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.11363v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A central goal in robot learning is to move beyond task-specific human data collection toward robots that improve through autonomous interaction. Yet fully autonomous learning remains difficult with current policies: sparse rewards and weak zero-shot exploration often prevent online learning from discovering successful behavior. As a first step towards fully autonomous learning, we propose the minimal-data adaptation regime, in which a pretrained robot policy must learn a new task from as little as one demonstration followed by autonomous online interaction. We establish that, although pretrained policies fail zero-shot on many new tasks, a single demonstration suffices to direct their behavioral prior to coarse task-following behavior, albeit with unreliable performance. From this insight, we isolate the key design principles required to convert coarse task-following into reliable task success. These include (1) the surprising efficacy of pretrained VLA representations to support sample-efficient value learning from online interaction (2) the sufficiency of residual policy learning to learn corrective behavior and (3) the need for careful data-balancing to prevent exploration collapse. As a representative of these principles, we propose MiDAS, a simple offline-to-online RL recipe that combines few-demonstration behavior cloning with value-based residual learning over frozen VLA representations. Across LIBERO and RoboCasa tasks, MiDAS substantially improves performance from single-demonstration initializations, including policies that succeed only rarely, validating the principles highlighted above. On a bimanual YAM platform, starting from a brittle initial policy, MiDAS improves task success after approximately six hours of online interaction.
items.author: Shreyas Kowshik, Sreyas Venkataraman, Leo Wang, Niharika Pant, Max Simchowitz, Aviral Kumar

items.title: Flipping Minds by Flipping Bits: Decision-Level Cognitive Hijacking of Large Language Models
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.25227v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely applied in high-stakes decision-making scenarios such as corporate strategy, and users are increasingly relying on their outputs. However, the deep integration of open-source model sharing ecosystems with LLM-powered critical decision-making applications also introduces critical risks: if an attacker can manipulate the model's cognitive stance, they can indirectly influence the judgments and actions of downstream decision-makers. This paper defines such threats as decision-level hijacking. Existing attacks fail to achieve targeted cognitive manipulation without triggering prohibited content or degrading model functionality. To fill this gap, this paper reveals that Bit-Flip Attacks (BFAs) can serve as an attack vector for inducing decision-level hijacking, requiring no real-time interaction or control over the training process, and only a minimal number of weight bits need to be flipped after deployment to achieve stealthy, low-cost, and persistent cognitive manipulation. Therefore, we propose CogBias, a cognitive bias injection framework for LLMs. CogBias converts subjective preferences into optimization signals via a differentiable sentiment evaluator, uses a multi-objective loss to jointly constrain multiple dimensions, and constructs BitScout to locate critical bits, achieving targeted cognitive intervention under an ultra-sparse flip budget. Experiments on Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, as well as on the commercial recommendation and controversial factual topic scenarios, demonstrate that flipping only a small number of bits stably induces significant stance shifts on target topics, while the impact on non-target tasks and overall output distribution is limited. This work demonstrates that minute perturbations to low-level weight data suffice to undermine the high-level value alignment of LLMs.
items.author: Yu Yan, Jiahao Chen, Siqi Lu, Yongjuan Wang, Ziming Zhao, Zhaoxuan Li, Tianyu Du, Qingjun Yuan, Shouling Ji

items.title: Machine Can Automatically Discover Parametric Functions to Model HEP Data
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.19750v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In HEP data analyses, finding an adequate function to model binned data has largely relied on a manual process: guess a functional form by intuition, fit, examine, then repeat until successful. We show that this iterative process can be automated by a machine using symbolic regression, which performs a data-driven search over function space without requiring prior knowledge of what an adequate function should look like. We present the SymbolFit package, which pairs symbolic regression with uncertainty modeling to target HEP analysis use cases, and demonstrate it on the CMS and ATLAS Run 2 dijet spectra: 560 independent seeded runs across seven simple fit configurations generated over 1000 functions fitting the spectra with $\chi^2/\text{NDF}\approx 1$, and 111 of the runs rediscovered the very dijet and UA2 functions used in published dijet searches.
items.author: Ho Fung Tsoi, Dylan Rankin, Cecile Caillol, Miles Cranmer, Sridhara Dasu, Javier Duarte, Philip Harris, Elliot Lipeles

items.title: Graph Partitioning with Demands: Generalized Conductance and its Applications
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.13218v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study various graph partitioning tasks subject to general demands. In Graph Partitioning with Demands (GPD), the goal is to delete minimum cost supply edge set so that each remaining component contains at most a prescribed fraction of the total demand. In the hierarchical analogue of this problem, Hierarchical Clustering with Demands (HCD), the goal is to build a hierarchy of clusters, charging each supply edge by the demand in the smallest cluster containing its endpoints.
  Our main general-graph results are approximation algorithms for GPD and HCD. For every fixed $0<\rho<\eta<1$, we give a polynomial-time bi-criteria algorithm for GPD whose components have demand at most $\eta \cdot W$ and cost at most $\mathcal{O}_{\rho,\eta}(\sqrt{\log n})$ times the optimum cost for threshold~$\rho$. This procedure can then be applied recursively to obtain an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log n})$-approximation for HCD. The algorithm for GPD itself uses a crucial subproblem called Generalized Conductance (GC), a new generalization of the Sparsest Cut.
  On supply trees, we show that GC can be solved exactly in polynomial time. We also give bi-criteria algorithms for GPD based on anchored-LP rounding and separator recursion, as well as a single-criterion $(4+\epsilon)$-approximation in $n^{O(1/\rho)}$ time. Moreover, through previous reduction, these GPD algorithms yield a $\frac{4e}{e-1}$-approximation for HCD on trees.
  We also prove that HCD and GPD and GC are SSEH-hard to approximate within any constant factor. On trees, assuming the Unique Games Conjecture (UGC), GPD is hard to approximate within a factor of $2-\epsilon$ by reduction from Vertex Cover, while HCD is hard to approximate within a factor of $1.0748$, by reduction from Min-Sum Vertex Cover.
items.author: Micha{\l} Szyfelbein, Dariusz Dereniowski

items.title: Tropical Circuits with Scalar Multiplication Gates
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.11540v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study tropical circuits with scalar multiplication gates, that is, algebraic circuits whose gates implement $\max$, $+$, or multiplication with a positive constant. For such circuits, we prove exponential size lower bounds for computing maximum weight directed spanning trees and maximum weight bipartite perfect matchings. As a corollary, we obtain an exponential size separation between monotone and non-monotone maxout neural networks, which generalize the popularly used ReLU neural networks. One conclusion from this is that neural network models with enforced convexity constraints, such as input-convex neural networks (ICNNs), sometimes need to be exponentially larger than their unrestricted counterparts in order to express the same functions.
items.author: Christoph Hertrich, Moritz Stargalla

items.title: How far do on-premises open LLMs get on Text-to-SQL? A cross-family size and technique frontier on BIRD
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.29733v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Organizations that cannot send data to a cloud API need to know how well self-hosted open-weight models perform on Text-to-SQL and which inexpensive techniques justify their compute. We benchmark Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct (7B, 14B, 32B) and CodeLlama-Instruct (7B, 13B) self-hosted at 16-bit precision, Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.3-70B through an FP8 API, and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B through a second API on the BIRD development split (n = 1534), with one zero-shot prompt and the official execution-accuracy comparison on read-only databases. We ablate lexical and embedding schema linking, execution-guided self-correction and self-consistency, and test every within-model recipe difference with exact McNemar tests, Holm correction over 30 tests and a database-clustered bootstrap. Qwen2.5-Coder reaches 42.6%, 52.0% and 54.9%; CodeLlama-7B and -13B reach 23.7% and 26.3%. Self-correction is the only component with a consistent gain: within a run it adds 1.2 to 4.4 points at 1.1 to 1.9 times the tokens, and it is significant after Holm correction for every model except Llama-3.3-70B. Schema linking never helps significantly; lexical linking costs Llama-3.3-70B 4.2 points, and an embedding linker with higher table recall does not differ detectably from no linking. Self-consistency, run for one model, changed accuracy by at most 0.13 points at about five times the tokens. One API provider dropped spaces next to digits; after a whitespace repair the same model scored 54.5% through the API and 54.9% self-hosted, so an apparent three-point serving gap was mostly this defect. This version corrects six defects of v1, including writable databases, a stricter-than-official metric and a truncated API arm, and withdraws the v1 claim of a quantization penalty of about 13 points; all numbers are re-scored or re-run. Code, per-item predictions and analysis scripts are released.
items.author: Vladimir Beskorovainyi

items.title: What Makes a Latent Thought Valid? Defining and Auditing Thought Representations in LLMs
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.27378v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet it writes steps as text and follows one reasoning path at a time, which limits the capabilities of such models. Latent reasoning methods replace these steps with continuous thought representations and claim that a thought representation substitutes for the written reasoning, compresses trajectories, distinguishes semantic content, and achieves superposition of multiple exploration paths at once. These claims concern the content of the thought representation, whereas the evaluations of these methods rely on downstream task accuracy, token counts, and analyses specific to each method. We formalize these claims as a valid thought representation space and prove that a space is valid if and only if its thought representations attain four properties, namely causality, minimality, separability, and stability, each of which follows from one claim. Translating these properties into four measures and auditing three training-free and three trained methods shows gaps in these claims that accuracy may not necessarily reveal. Training-free methods fail all four properties and do not encode the reasoning they are meant to replace, whereas trained methods generally improve substitution. The four properties and measures therefore provide a theoretically grounded evaluation beyond downstream task accuracy and expose failure modes that may guide future development of latent reasoning methods.
items.author: Fahd Seddik, Fatemeh Fard

items.title: FracEvent: Event-Camera Simulation via Fractional-Relaxation Pixel Dynamics
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.26636v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Event cameras asynchronously report brightness changes with microsecond-level temporal resolution, but real event data remain difficult to collect at scale because specialized sensors, careful synchronization, and task-specific annotations are required. Event-camera simulation is therefore important to event-based vision tasks. Most practical simulators build on contrast-threshold event generation, some with additional filtering, stochastic noise, or calibrated sensor parameters. While effective, such formulations can simplify the temporal structure produced by a pixel's recent response history. We introduce FracEvent, a physics-inspired sensor-side simulator with compact fractional-relaxation voltage dynamics. Given a log-intensity trajectory, FracEvent combines fast and slow response modes, emits ON/OFF events by localizing threshold crossings on the continuous voltage trajectory, and updates the event reference while retaining the mode states. This retained state links residual response to later event timing. We evaluate FracEvent through direct event-stream comparison and downstream transfer on image reconstruction and optical flow estimation. Across multiple datasets, FracEvent achieves leading results on multiple metrics in both evaluations, showing its practical value for event-camera simulation. Project page: https://bonaparte233.github.io/FracEvent/
items.author: Langyi Chen, Chuanzhi Xu, Haoxian Zhou, Pengfei Ye, Ziyu Luo, Haodong Chen, Qiang Qu, Xiaoming Chen, Weidong Cai

items.title: FairBED: Incorporating Fairness into Bayesian Experimental Design
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.23515v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Bayesian experimental design (BED) has traditionally focused exclusively on collecting data that is maximally informative, with little consideration of other desirable dataset characteristics, such as fairness. We therefore extend BED to target data that is both informative and fair. To this end, we introduce FairBED, which provides a formalism for the fairness of datasets themselves by measuring how compatible they are with a fair world, in which the target quantity we wish to learn about is unrelated to the sensitive attributes we want to be fair to. We then use this to construct practical fairness-aware BED objectives that maximise expected information gain about the target variables, while penalising information about sensitive attributes and/or their coupling with the target. We further extend FairBED to active learning, and show empirically that models trained on data gathered using FairBED provide improved fairness-accuracy trade-offs compared to randomly acquired data and conventional BED.
items.author: Marcel Hedman, Emily Alger, Brieuc Lehmann, Chris Holmes, Tom Rainforth

items.title: Regional summaries of Bayesian model uncertainty
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.21080v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Bayesian posterior uncertainty can be spread across many models that share the same substantive pattern. Lists of individual models can obscure this structure, while marginal summaries do not describe which configurations are jointly supported. We study how to represent joint model uncertainty through a compact collection of interpretable regions, each grouping models that share a specified pattern. We formulate this task as minimizing representation complexity subject to retaining a prescribed posterior mass within an analyst-supplied family. To address unknown regional probabilities, we develop Adaptive Regional Selection (ARS), which combines adaptive exploration and regional weight estimation with conservative and optimistic selection. These complementary problems identify a summary meeting the mass target and bound how much further its complexity could improve. Under valid regional bounds, we establish guarantees for retained mass, total-variation error, and suboptimality, together with conditions for certifying optimality. We also show that, under bounded within-region weight variation, sufficient sample counts for regional estimation need not grow with the number of represented models, and construct bounds that remain valid under adaptive sampling and stopping. Empirical studies illustrate regional summaries in Bayesian model averaging and Bayesian networks, examining retained mass, representation complexity, and certification.
items.author: Hanqing Li, Robert Nguyen, Xuewen Lu

items.title: Reward and Behavioral Measures of LLM Coordination in Dining Philosophers
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.07845v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Does high reward indicate productive coordination among language-model agents sharing resources? We examine this question in dining philosophers, where instances of the same model must acquire shared forks to eat. We evaluate seven model conditions across 630 episodes at five, ten, and fifteen philosophers, measuring scalar reward, deadlock, and meal throughput. At five philosophers, Mistral-Small 24B receives mean reward 0.827 while producing no meals. The reward decomposition explains this mismatch: avoiding deadlock earns a bonus without requiring meal production. To assess a policy trained with this reward, we compare the final checkpoint from a single Qwen3-14B group relative policy optimization (GRPO) training run with its base model. At five philosophers, the trained model has lower throughput (0.008 versus 0.020) and a higher deadlock rate in point estimates. Differences in mean episode reward are not statistically significant at any evaluated philosopher count. These findings show that the evaluated reward can assign high scores without task progress and support reporting behavioral measures alongside reward when comparing models and evaluating fine-tuned policies.
items.author: Najmul Hasan, Prashanth BusiReddyGari

items.title: Memory-Induced Tool-Drift in LLM Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.24941v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly combine long-term memory for personalization with tool calling for taking actions. We study a failure of this combination: personality-driven preferences stored in memory (e.g., cost-consciousness, impatience, risk tolerance) silently shifting tool-call parameters in contexts where they do not apply. We call this memory-induced tool-drift and stress-test it with MEMDRIFT, an iteratively refined benchmark of 105 scenarios spanning five bias dimensions and seven professional domains. Measured as excess parameter degradation over a neutral-memory baseline, biased memories in MEMDRIFT induce drift in all eight models we evaluate, raising degradation rates to 0.38--0.83 versus 0.05--0.12 for neutral memories. The drift persists under three widely used memory frameworks. A vulnerability audit of 6,062 tools across 288 MCP servers demonstrates that real-world tools are also susceptible to this failure mode. Mechanistically, we find that biased memories act as implicit steering vectors along the same direction as explicit behavioral instructions and draw attention away from task-relevant context. Neither prompt-based defenses nor relevance filters offer a complete solution, motivating defenses at the intersection of memory management and tool calling.
items.author: Mahavir Dabas, Jihyun Jeong, Ming Jin, Ruoxi Jia

items.title: PACE: Geometry-Aware Bridge Transport for Single-Cell Trajectory Inference
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.18587v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Single-cell trajectory inference from destructive time-course snapshots is fundamentally ill-posed: neither cross-time cell correspondences nor continuous trajectories are observed, so the snapshot distributions alone do not uniquely determine the underlying dynamics. Existing optimal transport and flow-based methods typically couple cells by Euclidean proximity at observed clock times, which can misalign trajectories when development is asynchronous and cells sampled at the same experimental time occupy different latent pseudotime stages. We propose PACE, a trajectory inference framework that recovers geometry-consistent continuous transport dynamics from destructive time-course snapshots through three coupled components. First, PACE constructs a state- and time-dependent anisotropic Riemannian metric that assigns low transport cost along locally supported tangent directions while penalizing normal velocity components. Second, it alternates between refining cross-time couplings under the induced path-action cost and fitting endpoint-preserving neural bridges between adjacent snapshots. Third, it distills the learned bridge dynamics into a global continuous-time velocity field over cellular states. Across seven controlled and biological datasets covering nine held-out reconstruction experiments, PACE achieves the strongest overall reconstruction performance, reducing MMD, Wasserstein-1 distance, and Wasserstein-2 distance by 23.7% on average relative to the strongest competing baseline. PACE also improves RNA-velocity alignment by 15.4% on an embryoid body differentiation benchmark, without requiring explicit cell pairing, lineage tracing, or RNA-velocity supervision during training. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/PACE.
items.author: Chenglei Yu, Chuanrui Wang, Bangyan Liao, Tailin Wu

items.title: Buffer-Parameterized Machine Learning Surrogate Models for Cross-Technology Signal Integrity Analysis and Optimization
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.18170v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Signal integrity (SI) analysis in printed circuit board (PCB) interconnects faces increasing complexity due to diverse integrated circuit (IC) buffer technologies, varying operating conditions, and manufacturing tolerances. Existing machine learning (ML) surrogate models for the prediction of SI metrics such as the inner eye contour, eye-height (EH), eye-width (EW), and transient waveform features often rely on fixed buffer parameters, limiting the adaptability across design and technology variations. This paper introduces a buffer-parameterized ML surrogate modeling methodology capable of handling cross-technology variations without retraining by treating IC buffer characteristics, e.g., clock frequency, supply voltage, rise/fall times, jitter, and internal resistors and capacitors, as model inputs in addition to the PCB parameters. To identify the optimal surrogate architecture for this high-dimensional space, tree-based methods (RFR/GBM), kernel methods (SVR/KRR), Gaussian process regression (GPR), and neural networks are compared. The buffer-parameterized approach is validated using a complex interconnect with a total of 44 design parameters. In addition to demonstrating strong generalization, the results show that neural networks outperform other ML models on large datasets, while the anisotropic GPR excels in low-data regimes. Finally, the practical value of the ML surrogate models is demonstrated through a cross-technology design space exploration and optimization scenario, which indicates large computational speedups for eye mask compliance checking compared to simulation.
items.author: Julian With\"oft, Werner John, Emre Ecik, Ralf Br\"uning, J\"urgen G\"otze

items.title: Large Language Models over Networks: Collaborative Intelligence under Resource Constraints
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.08626v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming society, powering applications from smartphone assistants to autonomous driving. Yet cloud-based LLM services alone cannot serve a growing class of applications, including those operating under intermittent connectivity, sub-second latency budgets, data-residency constraints, or sustained high-volume inference. On-device deployment is in turn constrained by limited computation and memory. No single endpoint can deliver high-quality service across this spectrum. This article focuses on collaborative intelligence, a paradigm in which multiple independent LLMs distributed across device and cloud endpoints collaborate at the task level through natural language or structured messages. Such collaboration strives for superior response quality under heterogeneous resource constraints spanning computation, memory, communication, and cost across network tiers. We present collaborative inference along two complementary and composable dimensions: vertical device-cloud collaboration and horizontal multi-agent collaboration, which can be combined into hybrid topologies in practice. We then examine learning to collaborate, addressing the training of routing policies and the development of cooperative capabilities among LLMs. Finally, we identify open research challenges including scaling under resource heterogeneity and trustworthy collaborative intelligence.
items.author: Liangqi Yuan, Wenzhi Fang, Shiqiang Wang, H. Vincent Poor, Christopher G. Brinton

items.title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments
items.summary:
arXiv:2605.06520v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Regulatory approval of products in high-stakes domains such as drug development requires statistical evidence of safety and efficacy through large-scale randomized controlled trials. However, the high financial cost of these trials may deter developers who lack absolute certainty in their product's efficacy, ultimately stifling the development of `moonshot' products that could offer high social utility. To address this inefficiency, in this paper, we introduce a statistical protocol for experimentation where the product developer (the agent) conducts a randomized controlled trial sequentially and the regulator (the principal) partially subsidizes its cost. By modeling the protocol using a belief Markov decision process, we show that the agent's optimal strategy can be found efficiently using dynamic programming. Further, we show that the social utility is a piecewise linear and convex function over the subsidy level the principal selects, and thus the socially optimal subsidy can also be found efficiently using divide-and-conquer. Simulation experiments using publicly available data on antibiotic development and approval demonstrate that our statistical protocol can be used to increase social utility by more than $35$$\%$ relative to standard, non-sequential protocols.
items.author: Ander Artola Velasco, Stratis Tsirtsis, Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez

items.title: Data-Efficient Indentation Size Effect Mitigation in Steels Using Machine Learning and a Physics-Constrained Neural Network
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.27775v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Shallow nanoindentation, needed for thin layers, individual phases and small volumes, gives hardness inflated by the indentation size effect (ISE). The Nix-Gao correction reduces this inflation but requires deep indentations of the same material, often impossible in such samples. We present a data-efficient workflow, trained on a few reference materials, that predicts a high-load reference hardness from a single shallow indentation. Seven models were trained on 703 indentations (5-350 mN) on three steels (2.0-6.5 GPa): Ridge regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, two feed-forward networks, and two physics-constrained neural networks (PCNNs) that apply a bounded learned correction q as H_app/sqrt(1+q). Over five seeds, models were tested on an external steel not used for training and indented at different loads, in leave-one-steel-out folds, and on fused silica, an out-of-domain material where all models failed. Random Forest and XGBoost, the best on the development set, transferred worst over all loads (MAPE 10.2 and 8.5%), whereas Ridge regression, the PCNNs and one feed-forward network reached 3.7-4.8%; with three training steels, development-set accuracy thus did not indicate accuracy on an unseen steel. From only the external steel's 3-15 mN indentations, the smooth (non-tree) models estimated the reference within 0.03-0.19 GPa on average. The PCNNs matched the linear baseline within the training hardness range and were the most accurate for a held-out steel softer than the training steels, but failed for a harder one. The workflow uses no steel-specific inputs and can be retrained for other material classes.
items.author: Radmir Karamov, Tagir Karamov

items.title: Integrative neurocybernetic modeling in the era of large-scale neuroscience
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.23903v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large-scale neuroscience is generating rich datasets across animals, brain areas, and behavioral contexts, yet our modeling efforts remain fragmented across isolated experiments. We argue that understanding behavior requires integrative neurocybernetic models: understandable dynamical models that capture the closed-loop coupling of brain, body, and environment, treat the brain as a controller pursuing latent objectives, represent structured variation across scales, and scale to heterogeneous datasets. Such models shift the goal from predicting neural recordings in isolation to inferring the organizing principles that govern neural and behavioral dynamics. We outline a practical route toward this goal by combining nonlinear state-space models and meta-dynamical extensions with scalable inference, knowledge distillation, and mixed open- and closed-loop training. By pooling complementary constraints from recordings, behavior, perturbations, and anatomy, integrative neurocybernetic models can provide statistical amplification, few-shot generalization, and mechanistic insight into shared dynamical structure, individual variation, and the control objectives that govern behavior. This agenda offers a model-centric path from fragmented data to a mechanistic science of how brains produce behavior.
items.author: Il Memming Park, Gonzalo G. de Polavieja, Ayesha Vermani, Juan \'Alvaro Gallego, Kathleen Esfahany, Shreya Saxena, Guillaume Hennequin, Michael Orger, Auke Ijspeert, Matthew Dowling, Daniel McNamee, Srinivas C. Turaga, Zachary Mainen, Alfonso Renart, Joseph J. Paton

items.title: Best of both worlds: Stochastic & adversarial best-arm identification
items.summary:
arXiv:2604.14860v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study bandit best-arm identification with arbitrary and potentially adversarial rewards. A simple random uniform learner obtains the optimal rate of error in the adversarial scenario. However, this type of strategy is suboptimal when the rewards are sampled stochastically. Therefore, we ask: Can we design a learner that performs optimally in both the stochastic and adversarial problems while not being aware of the nature of the rewards? First, we show that designing such a learner is impossible in general.
